public_rationale: Contemporary experiments substantiate serious chess-rule failures. They do not establish Marcus’s explanation of those failures. Later intervention research also shows that next-token training can produce usable board representations in specialized models. Neither result settles the causal claim about contemporary GPT.
limitations: A failure to follow rules does not by itself reveal the model’s internal representations.
The counterevidence concerns specialized later models, not the same GPT system.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: GPT's failure to stick to the rules of chess, even when it plays a decent game, reflects the same problem: correlations are fragile and cannot be counted on.
conditions: in the context of GPT playing chess

statement.excerpt: It’s the same problem: correlations are fragile, and you can’t count on them.

from_speaker: doesn’t really model the rules of chess well enough to stick to them
our_interpretation: The claim concerns the cause of rule violations by GPT systems contemporary with the October 2023 post.
The plain reading is that reliance on learned correlations explains recurring illegal moves. Demonstrating illegal moves alone does not establish this explanation.
Controlled changes to board-state information, training, or internal representations could distinguish this explanation from other causes.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary GPT chess evaluations establish recurring rule violations, and controlled experiments identify reliance on correlations without adequate board-and-rule representations as a cause.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Controlled experiments on the relevant systems establish usable board-and-rule representations and show that the attributed absence of those representations does not explain the violations.

evidence.publisher: arXiv; Mu-Tien Kuo, Chih-Chung Hsueh, and Richard Tzong-Han Tsai
evidence.explanation: The experiments document substantial problems following chess rules in GPT-3.5-turbo-0301. They support the behavioral premise, but do not isolate reliance on correlations as its cause.

The author reports interventions in chess-model activations that change moves in line with altered board states. This challenges a blanket opposition between statistical training and internal models, but does not settle the cause of failures in the GPT systems Marcus discussed.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Controlled experiments on preserved contemporary GPT versions that measure board representations and test whether changing those representations explains or removes recurring illegal moves.
